### Composite pressure vessels and tank structure

**This cluster is where the vehicle's actual failure lives.** Its literature divides between the design and analysis of filament wound vessels and their response to damage. **Of its 332 titles from 2015 onward, 37 name burst, 44 impact or damage, 14 the liner and 33 hydrogen or natural gas storage, and none names permeation.** The modern literature has moved toward vehicle gas storage, and the question this vessel posed, failure under gas pressurisation after a hydrostatic proof, is taken up under Thin Subjects in the Source Base.

### Nozzles, thrust coefficient and performance

**The most settled body of work in the survey, and the one the article leans on most confidently.** Thrust coefficient, characteristic velocity and expansion ratio relations have not changed and are not in dispute, which is what allows this article to re-derive the engine's geometry from three published numbers and check the result against a fourth. **Where a literature is settled, an independent derivation is evidence about the source rather than about the physics**, and that is how the derivations in this article should be read.

### Pressure-fed feed systems and stage sizing

**This is the cluster the article's keystone sits in, and its size is unremarkable.** That is itself informative, because a relation this article treats as the whole design supports no distinctive literature of its own. Pressure-fed stage design is a solved problem in the sense that the governing relation is elementary and has been known since the first liquid stages, so the literature treats it as a sizing input rather than a research question. What activity there is concentrates on the parts the elementary relation omits. **Of the cluster's 504 titles, 203 name pressurisation, 112 slosh, 41 settling or gravity and 9 a regulator.** Those are the areas where this vehicle's published record is thinnest, which is a fair indication of where its remaining engineering risk lay.

### Ablative materials and nozzle erosion

**This cluster explains why an ablative nozzle was a reasonable choice and not a cheap one.** Its titles measure and model the charring, recession and erosion of silica, quartz and carbon phenolic and of graphite throats. **It holds work on reducing erosion as well as predicting it, among it three titles on the boundary-layer control of graphite throat erosion**, and the vehicle took the other route, holding thrust in the flow control rather than protecting the throat. The article does not compare its erosion figures with published rates, and this cluster is the literature in which that comparison would be made.

### Attitude control, separation and stage subsystems

**This cluster covers the conventional two thirds of the vehicle, and the article uses it mainly to establish that those parts were conventional.** Of the cluster's 166 titles on cold gas systems, pyrotechnic separation and thrust vector control, 54 predate 1998 and the earliest is from 1961, which is the record of a settled engineering practice. **Naming that explicitly matters**, because an article organised around a novel keystone will otherwise imply that the whole vehicle was novel.

### Upper stages, kick stages and orbit insertion

**At 225 records this is the smallest of the nine central clusters, and that is the clearest evidence that the pop-up stage concept did not take hold.** The nine central clusters are named in What the Shape of the Survey Says above. **Of the cluster's 80 titles from 2015 onward, none names responsiveness, a military mission or a pop-up mission, and eight name a kick stage, rideshare or a small satellite**, the rest serving heavy-lift exploration stages, hybrid-propellant small stages, guidance and the disposal of spent stages. **The requirement left no continuing literature under that name.**

### Cryogenic propellants and cryogenic engines

**Present as the alternative the programme rejected, and the comparison is what the cluster is for.** Cryogenic propulsion dominates upper stage performance on specific impulse and loses on density impulse and on storability, which are the two criteria this vehicle was designed against. **Of the cluster's 110 titles from 2015 onward, 47 name tanks, insulation, stratification, boil-off or storage**, which is the effort to fix the two properties that made cryogenics unsuitable here.

### Launch vehicle dynamics, loads and flight control

**Included because the integral structure is a load path as well as a pressure vessel.** A conventional stage separates those functions and this one did not, so the literature on launch loads, structural dynamics and their coupling into control is directly relevant to whether the single-piece structure was a good idea. The public record contains no loads analysis for this vehicle, so this cluster establishes what questions would have to be answered rather than answering any of them.

### Programme, cost and mission analysis

**This cluster is where the article's stated objective lives and where its keystone cannot follow.** The programme called itself low cost propulsion and the mass relation this article derives says nothing about cost. The literature here is concerned with development cost, reliability and the economics of launch, and it is the body of work that would have to be consulted to judge whether the pressure-fed choice actually paid. **The article does not make that judgement**, and the Where the Framing Breaks Down section says so.

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**The keystone in this article is a mass relation, and there are three places where reading the vehicle
through it misleads.**

**First, the relation says nothing about cost, and cost was the stated objective.** The programme called
itself low cost propulsion and the word appears in the title of its founding paper\[[Anderson et al. 1998][research_anderson_1998]\]. A pressure-fed
stage is chosen because turbomachinery is expensive to develop, not because the mass relation favours
it, and by the mass relation alone a pump-fed stage wins comfortably. **The article derives why the
pressure-fed choice was survivable and not why it was made**, and those are different questions.

**Second, the relation treats the tank as a membrane and the failure was not a membrane failure.** A
vessel that passes a hydrostatic proof at 150 percent and fifty cycles to its operating pressure and
then fails during a helium pressurisation points to liners, joints, bosses, permeation, the adhesive
bond, or the difference between a liquid and a gas as the pressurising medium. **None of those appear
anywhere in the keystone**, so the keystone cannot explain the outcome of the
programme.

**Third, treating the vehicle as a technology demonstrator understates how much of it was ordinary.**
The cold gas attitude control, the linear shaped charge separation, the gimballed engine and the helium
pressurisation are all conventional, and the novelty was concentrated in the tank and the propellant.
**An article organised around the keystone naturally over-reports the novel parts**, and a reader
should carry away that this was a mostly conventional stage with two unusual choices rather than a
wholly experimental vehicle.

**A fourth caution concerns the designation itself.** The analysis would be unchanged if the allocation
were shown to have been intended for something else, so the designation is a filing convenience rather
than a fact about the hardware.

## The Source Base

**41 curated sources carry the argument, and the 38 of them that are research records also stand in the survey, whose 8,226 records map the field.** The article keeps the two roles apart in how it cites them, the curated sources for statements and the cluster rows for the shape of the literature.

**38 of the 41 are primary or canonical technical sources**, being conference papers, journal
papers, technical reports and design criteria monographs. Two are the designation reference that
supplies the allocation dates and the disputed pairing, and one is a textbook. **24 of the 38 technical
sources are contemporary with the programme**, falling between 1997 and 2009. The count is reported
alongside the fraction because adding a canonical source from 1967 lowers the fraction while leaving the
contemporary count untouched.

**20 of the 41 come from the NASA Technical Reports Server, and five more, conference papers cited here in their published form, are deposited there as well**, which is the single fact that made this
article possible. The programme was run by a contractor under NASA management, so its engine papers,
its programme overview, its incident report, its pressurant tank development and the design criteria
its engineers worked from are all in one open register. The structures paper is held in full by the
Defense Technical Information Center as component ADP020323 of the proceedings of the 12th International
Conference on Composite Structures of November 2003.

**The NASA design criteria monographs supply most of the canonical relations.** Eight are
cited, covering self-cooled combustion chambers, pressurisation systems, injectors, nozzles, metal
tanks, regulators and valves, flexible lines, and propellant slosh loads. **They are contemporary with
the practice this vehicle inherited rather than with the vehicle**, and they are primary documents
rather than textbook summaries, which is why they are preferred here to a modern reference that would
say the same thing with less authority.

**The two engine papers of 2000 were presented at the same conference and print different operating
points.** The engine design and test results and the catalyst bed instability analysis were both given
at the 36th Joint Propulsion Conference in July 2000. The first prints 10,000 pounds of thrust at 500
pounds per square inch, the second 9,480 at 485, and the 1999 papers a third version at a mixture ratio
of 6.0. **Reading any one of them alone gives a falsely settled account of the engine.**

**The structural argument rests on a single paper in a structures journal**, which is a concentration
worth naming. The operating pressure, the proof and burst factors, the tank volumes, the strain data and
the proof test date all trace to it. The 1999 overview paper describes the same structure and its
subscale programme in outline and agrees on the single-piece design and on the liner serving as the
winding mandrel.

**One source is an unfinished paper and it is used for several subsystem details that appear nowhere
else.** NASA's Technical Reports Server holds it as a 1999 paper for the Hydrogen Peroxide Propulsion
conference of November 1999, under contract NAS8-98040, and it carries an unwritten section heading, an
uncorrected edit and a note asking a co-author to finish a section. **Its helium pressurant tank is
independently corroborated by a NASA Marshall paper**, which describes a different liner, so the
corroboration extends to the component and not to every figure.

**The research survey holds 8,226 records, of which 8,206 resolve through Crossref digital object identifiers and 20 through NASA's Technical Reports Server.** **The median publication year is 2013.** Of the 8,226 records, 2,523 were published before 2000, being 30.7 percent, and 3,820 in 2015 or later, being 46.4 percent.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is a NASA Technical Reports Server citation or its digital object identifier carries the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. **By that rule 416 of the 8,226 records are report primaries, being 5.1 percent.**

**The rule excludes the conference and journal papers of the people who built the stage**, among them the 2000 engine design paper \[[Ross et al. 2000][research_ross_2000]\] and the 2004 structures paper \[[Guerrero et al. 2004][research_guerrero_2004]\]. **5.1 percent is therefore a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand**, and the 20 Technical Reports Server records cited in the argument are the primaries that carry it.

### Thin Subjects

**Five subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| propellant density as a stage-sizing lever | density impulse, bulk density, propellant density | 4 |
| tank mass against pressure, volume and specific strength | tank mass, tank weight, tankage weight, tank structural weight, specific strength, strength to weight | 1 |
| tank and vessel materials in contact with concentrated peroxide | peroxide, H2O2, HTP or high test, together with tank, tankage, vessel or compatibility | 5 |
| catalyst bed life and instability | catalyst bed, catalytic bed or silver screen, together with life, instability, degradation, failure, deactivation, poisoning or endurance | 3 |
| helium pressurisation of a composite vessel | helium, together with composite, overwrapped, COPV or filament wound | 0 |

**The keystone itself has one record.** The relation between tank mass, pressure, volume and specific strength is elementary, and the only title in the survey that carries any of these terms is a method for estimating a launch vehicle tank's structural weight \[[Hutchinson and Olds 2004][research_hutchinson_olds_2004]\]. **This is the kind of thin that a settled relation produces**, and the article's claim stands on the derivation rather than on a literature.

**Propellant density as a sizing lever has four records, the newest from 2009**, although density is the first of the two levers this vehicle pulled.

**No title in the survey names helium together with a composite vessel**, which is the combination under which the integral tank failed, so the failure mode the article locates in the tank has no literature of its own under that name.

**Peroxide compatibility of tank and vessel materials has five records, all from 2001 to 2004**, and catalyst bed life and instability has three, one of which is this engine's own catalyst bed instability paper. **These are the two subjects the choice of peroxide made critical, and the later literature returns to them rarely**, the compatibility titles ending in 2004 and the catalyst bed titles numbering two after this engine's paper.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject.** The subject is rocket engines and motors and their components, launch vehicles and stages, propellants as propellants, pressure vessels and propellant tanks, feed and pressurisation systems, ablative materials, reaction control and separation by thrusters and pyrotechnics, and the testing of rocket hardware. Every record is filed under a named literature, and the survey has no residual cluster.

**Much of the vocabulary this subject depends on also names something else, and a record that shares only such a word or a distant application is excluded.** Combustion chamber also names the cylinders of diesel and gasoline engines, the combustors and film-cooled blades of gas turbines and the furnaces of boilers. Catalyst bed also names the reactors of chemical plants, and peroxide decomposition also serves environmental and biochemical work. Tank also names aircraft and road vehicle fuel tanks, ship and industrial storage tanks, and the integral wing tanks whose sealants and ullage chemistry fill a literature of their own. Attitude control also names the control of satellites by reaction wheels, control moment gyroscopes and magnetic torquers, and thrust vector control also names the nozzles of aircraft and airships. Rocket also names the guided and unguided rockets of artillery and the sleds of track testing, liquid propellant also names the charges of guns, and nozzle also names the metering nozzles of flow measurement. Electric, laser, beamed and fusion propulsion are excluded as distant applications, because they share no hardware with a chemical stage. Carbon and epoxy laminates studied for their own sake, and filament-wound products whose subject is a distant application such as a racquet, a rotor blade or a flywheel, are excluded as well. Correction, retraction and removal notices and dictionary entries are excluded, because a survey counts research works and those are editorial events or parts of works. A review of a book, a reference or definition entry, a notice such as front matter, an editorial or a news item, signed or unsigned, a patent abstract, an abstract reprinted by an abstract journal or in another journal's abstract section, and a second deposit of a document already counted are not admitted either, since none of them is a research work in its own right.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Filament-wound and composite tubes and pipes under internal pressure are kept as the tank's neighbouring mechanics, and so are cryogenic properties and proof testing of composite laminates. Combustion chamber and film cooling studies whose application the title does not state, dual-throat thrust-vectoring nozzles, the decomposition chemistry of peroxide, missile thrust vector control, underwater rockets and air-breathing launch concepts are kept because they share the subject's physics or vehicle class. A reader may weigh them accordingly.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.**

## Epistemic State

### Historical Fact

**These statements are drawn from the primary record and are not in dispute.**

The Air Force Research Laboratory began a formal pop-up upper stage effort in 1997 under the name
Modular Insertion Stage. Studies sponsored that year concluded that high concentration hydrogen
peroxide with a hydrocarbon fuel best met the storability and non toxicity requirements\[[USFE X-42][ref_x42_parsch]\]. Orbital
Sciences Corporation held the contract to design, develop and demonstrate the resulting Upper Stage
Flight Experiment, under NASA Marshall Space Flight Center management in cooperation with the
laboratory, and NASA dates its start to December 1997\[[McNeal and Anderson 1999][research_mcneal_1999]\].

The engine burned ninety percent hydrogen peroxide with JP-8 at a mixture ratio of 4.7, produced
10,000 pounds of vacuum thrust at a chamber pressure of 500 pounds per square inch absolute with a
nozzle expansion ratio of 40, and had a design burn time of 200 seconds at a flowrate of 36.0 pounds per
second\[[Ross et al. 2000][research_ross_2000]\]. Two development test series were run at the E-3 test cell at the Stennis Space Center in
campaigns from late 1998 to early 2000, the first on 85 percent peroxide and the second on 90 percent.
The first series accumulated 300 seconds of bipropellant operation and over 700 seconds on a single
catalyst bed, and demonstrated multiple restarts and throttling to 10 percent in monopropellant mode and
20 percent in bipropellant mode. A 140 second test was run on 19 May 1999. A 150 second test concluded
the second series.

A low frequency catalyst bed instability appeared as the peroxide flow rose through about 12 pounds per
second, about one third of the design rate, in monopropellant testing, and was removed by a change of
combustion chamber configuration\[[Johnson et al. 2000][research_johnson_anderson_2000]\].

The integral structure was an all-composite assembly of both propellant tanks, with a common bulkhead,
bonded into a filament wound skirt. Its tanks enclosed 44.8 and 15.5 cubic feet at a maximum expected
operating pressure of 1,100 pounds per square inch absolute, the stage was designed for a 110 second
burn, and the structure was hydrostatically proof tested at Chandler, Arizona between 15 and 17 April
2003 to 150 percent of that pressure and then cycled 50 times to it\[[Guerrero et al. 2004][research_guerrero_2004]\].

The X-42A designation was allocated in late 1997 or early 1998 to an expendable demonstrator for pop-up
upper stage technology and was not used in any subsequent official announcement. In 2002 the laboratory
and industry used X-42 unofficially for a reusable launch vehicle demonstrator concept based on Orbital
Sciences' Multi-Role Reusable Vehicle, powered by a single RS-27 engine and able to carry a Common Aero
Vehicle\[[USFE X-42][ref_x42_parsch]\].

An overpressurisation incident occurred at the Stennis Space Center in December 2000 during work on
advanced catalyst beds and high concentration peroxide, damaging facility infrastructure and test
hardware\[[Ross et al. 2001][research_ross_2001]\].

The suborbital flight test was scheduled for 2001 in 1999\[[Anderson et al. 1999][research_anderson_usfe]\] and for 2002 in 2000\[[Johnson et al. 2000][research_johnson_anderson_2000]\], and no flight
took place.

### Verified by Independent Derivation

**Every input below is a value one of the primary papers reports, and every output was computed in
this article rather than quoted from anywhere.** The qualification is made once here and not repeated
against each item.

The throat area of 11.06 square inches, throat diameter of 3.75 inches and exit diameter of 23.7 inches
come from the contraction ratio of 7.1 with a chamber diameter of ten inches, agree with the 3.74 and
23.7 inch figures on the 1999 drawing, and the exit diameter sits inside the stated 40 inch engine
envelope.

The 110 second flight burn at 36.0 pounds per second is 3,960 pounds of propellant, which at the stated
mixture ratio and the assumed densities fills 85.5 percent of the 60.3 cubic feet the published tank
volumes enclose.

The characteristic velocity of 4,943 feet per second and thrust coefficient of 1.808 come from the
published thrust, chamber pressure and flowrate, and the thrust coefficient sits just below the ideal
vacuum value for the stated expansion ratio, as a real nozzle must.

The chamber pressure history of the 140 second test implies a throat-average erosion rate of 0.00050
inches per second, below the allowance, although the paper's own reading of the same test is that local
erosion with that injector was too severe at that mixture ratio.

The catalyst bed frontal diameter of 9.72 inches comes from the oxidiser flow and the bed mass flux,
and fits inside the ten inch chamber with three percent to spare. **Those numbers were reported in
different sections for different purposes and they agree.**

The chamber Mach number of 0.083 comes from the contraction ratio through the isentropic area relation,
and places the chamber within a tenth of a percent of stagnation temperature, the condition
that the paper's autoignition requirement calls for.

The ideal vacuum thrust coefficient of 1.884 at a ratio of specific heats of 1.20 and 1.835 at 1.25 is
the area ratio relation solved at an expansion ratio of 40. **The implied 1.808 sits below both, and
losses can only push a real nozzle downward.**

The 195 pound per square inch design pressure difference across the common bulkhead with the oxidiser
tank higher covers the 136 pound per square inch catalyst bed drop that only the oxidiser passes
through.

The isotensoid winding angle of 54.7 degrees follows from the two-to-one ratio of hoop to axial membrane
load in a pressurised cylinder alone.

The vacuum thrust coefficient falls by under one percent as the expansion ratio drops from 40 to 32.7,
which is the change corresponding to a full 200 second burn at the allowable erosion rate.

### Analysis

**These are engineering conclusions drawn in this article from the relations shown.**

Tank mass for a pressure vessel is proportional to the product of pressure and enclosed volume divided
by the material specific strength, with shape entering only through a constant between 1.5 and 2, so a
pressure-fed stage pays a penalty proportional to its propellant volume that does not diminish with
scale.

The tank mass fraction relation has three levers, being pressure, propellant bulk density and material
specific strength, and this vehicle pulled the second and third simultaneously. On density impulse the
peroxide and JP-8 combination beats liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen by more than a factor of two and
falls about eleven percent short of nitrogen tetroxide with monomethylhydrazine.

The specific strength advantage of filament wound carbon and epoxy over aluminium alloy 2219-T87 is a
factor of between seven and eleven, which on the ideal membrane relation at the published operating
pressure is the difference between a tank costing about 1.2 percent of the propellant it holds and one
costing about 8.8 percent.

Because cavitating venturis fix the mass flow, the product of chamber pressure and throat area is
constant, so thrust follows the thrust coefficient alone and a 22.5 percent growth in throat area
produces about a one percent change in thrust. **The ablative nozzle and the cavitating venturi are a single
design decision.**

The instability onset at about 12 pounds per second lies above the 10 and 20 percent throttle points and
below design flow, so the chamber change was needed to pass through one third of design flow on the way
to full thrust, and the record does not tie it to the throttling result.

### Inference

**These are reasoned conclusions that the record permits but does not state.**

**The one percent non-closure of the 2000 engine table is a remnant of the 1999 design point.** The
1999 table pairs the same thrust and flowrate with 278 seconds, which closes, and the 2000 table changed
the specific impulse and the mixture ratio and left thrust and flowrate as they were. Neither paper says
so.

**The X-42A allocation and the Upper Stage Flight Experiment are contemporaneous rather than merely
adjacent.** The allocation falls in late 1997 or early 1998, and NASA dates the start of the experiment
with Orbital Sciences to December 1997\[[McNeal and Anderson 1999][research_mcneal_1999]\]. **This distinguishes the X-42 case from the X-41 case**, where
the designation preceded its programme by years. The doubt about X-42 is of a different kind. The pairing
is not anachronistic, but no official use ever confirmed it.

**One date in this argument is weaker than the rest.** The January 1998 request for proposals rests on
the designation survey alone, and no Air Force document stating it is available. The argument does not
depend on it, since the allocation window and the contract start are independently attested.

**The two X-42 usages are related through the sponsoring organisation rather than through the
hardware.** Both trace to the Air Force Research Laboratory Space Vehicles Directorate in the same
period. This is a plausible common cause and it is not documented as one.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**The stage's inert mass was never released**, so this article gives achievable velocity increment as a
family across assumed inert and payload masses rather than as a number. Across inert masses from 600
to 1,000 pounds and payloads from none to 2,000 pounds, with the 110 second load, the family spans
roughly 2,270 to 5,470 metres per second. **The inert mass is the one quantity that would turn that
family into an answer**, and it is the quantity a cancelled programme never publishes.

**Why the tanks were sized for a 110 second burn when the engine was rated for 200 is not explained**,
nor why their volume ratio corresponds to a mixture ratio near 5.0 rather than the 4.7 of the engine
table.

**The decomposition temperature is derived here with constant specific heats and is an upper bound**,
giving 780 degrees Celsius. The direction of the error is known from the assumption, since the heat
capacity of steam rises with temperature, and no source cited here prints a measured value to compare
it with, so the calculation can only bound the temperature.

**The pressurant figures are isothermal lower bounds.** Real blowdown cools the gas, so the 25.4
kilograms and the 13.5 cubic foot bottle are the least that would have worked, not estimates of what was
built. No figure for the pressurant load appears anywhere in the record.

**The catalyst bed has no stated life.** Bed pressure drop is reported as rising with accumulated run
time and no limit is given, so the one number that would say whether the engine was ready to fly is
missing.

**The cause of the tank failure was never disclosed**, and the possibilities are set out under Where the
Framing Breaks Down.

**Whether the December 2000 Stennis incident involved this engine is not established.** The abstract
places it at the same centre during peroxide work in the same period and says no more, and this article
says no more either.

**No flight is recorded**, and the flight test discussion treats that as an argument
from silence.

**Whether the X-42 designation properly belongs to this vehicle is not settled**, and the authoritative
survey declines to settle it, recording that the designation is not tied to a specific programme or
vehicle.

### On Sources Used With Reservation

**One source used in the Dependent Systems section is an unfinished paper.** NASA's Technical Reports
Server holds it as a 1999 paper under contract NAS8-98040, and it carries an unwritten section, an
uncorrected edit and an editorial note to a co-author\[[Anderson et al. 1999][research_anderson_usfe]\]. **It is the only source for several subsystem
details**, being the nitrogen attitude control tank pressure, the separation arrangement and the
propellant management thrusters. Its helium pressurant tank is corroborated\[[DeLay and Munafo 2001][research_delay_2001]\], although the
corroborating paper describes a metallic permeation barrier where this one describes a plastic liner.
**A reader should treat the uncorroborated subsystem figures as the weakest quantitative claims in this
article.**

**The end of the programme rests on one secondary source.** The tank failure, the second prototype's
leakage and the 2006 and 2007 schedule appear only in the designation survey\[[USFE X-42][ref_x42_parsch]\], which cites an Air Force
Research Laboratory release of August 2005 that is not available here.

### Assumed Values

**These values are not stated by any source cited here and are assumed for the derivations.** They are
the propellant densities of 1.387 grams per cubic centimetre for 90 percent peroxide and 0.804 for JP-8,
the bulk densities and specific impulses of the three comparison combinations in the density impulse
table, the specific strength range of $1.0 \times 10^{6}$ to $1.6 \times 10^{6}$ joules per kilogram for
filament wound carbon and epoxy, the reaction enthalpy, latent heat and heat capacities of the
decomposition balance, the ratios of specific heats of 1.20 and 1.25 for the combustion products and 1.4
for nitrogen, the gas temperature of 300 kelvin for helium and nitrogen, and the inert masses and
payloads of the velocity family.

### On Information Postdating the Editorial Date

This article is written from current knowledge. Where the contemporary survey above reports work
published after the editorial date, it is included because this series surveys the contemporary
literature rather than reconstructing what was knowable in 2025.

## Out of Scope

**The Military Spaceplane programme as a whole** is treated only as the context that generated the
pop-up stage requirement. Its architecture studies, its funding history and its cancellation are the
subject of the series articles on the vehicles it produced.

**The 2002 reusable launch vehicle concept** is treated as evidence about the designation rather than as
a vehicle. Its aerodynamics, its RS-27 propulsion and the Multi-Role Reusable Vehicle lineage it derives
from are not analysed here.

**Hydrogen peroxide as a monopropellant for satellite propulsion** is surveyed but not derived. The
article's keystone is a stage mass relation, and monopropellant attitude control systems answer a
different question.

**The chemistry of peroxide decomposition** is taken as given. Catalyst formulation, screen metallurgy
and the kinetics of the decomposition are named where they bear on bed life and are not developed.

**Materials compatibility testing for concentrated peroxide** is surveyed and not derived, although it
is very likely the discipline that decided this programme's outcome.

**The economics of low cost access to space** are outside the article. The programme's stated objective
was cost and this article derives mass, and the gap between those is discussed under Where the Framing
Breaks Down rather than closed.

## Conclusion

**The Upper Stage Flight Experiment asked whether a pressure-fed stage could be made light enough to be
worth flying, and the hardware it produced shows that the answer is yes and that the hard part is
somewhere else.**

The mass relation that governs a pressure vessel leaves three levers, and this vehicle pulled two of
them at once. A propellant combination with a bulk density of 1.23 grams per cubic centimetre shrank the
tanks that a pressure-fed architecture must hold at several hundred pounds per square inch, and a
filament wound carbon and epoxy structure held them at a specific strength between seven and eleven
times that of the aluminium alternative. **Together those choices turn the pressure-fed penalty from
disqualifying into marginal**, and the engine that resulted ran for more than seven hundred seconds on a
single catalyst bed, restarted repeatedly, throttled to a tenth of its design flow, came through a
catalyst bed instability that a chamber change removed, and would hold its thrust within about one
percent while its throat eroded by 22 percent over a full design burn, because the flow control made
thrust nearly independent of the geometry that was changing.

**The programme was then destroyed by the component it existed to prove.** A tank that had passed a
hydrostatic proof at 1,650 pounds per square inch and fifty cycles to its 1,100 pound operating pressure
failed during a helium pressurisation test and took the engine with it, a second article leaked, and no
flight ever followed\[[Guerrero et al. 2004][research_guerrero_2004]\]\[[USFE X-42][ref_x42_parsch]\]. **The failure is more
informative than a launch failure would have been**, because it locates the difficulty precisely in the
composite pressure vessel and not in the propulsion, the propellant choice or the mass relation that
justified them.

**The designation is a separate story and a worse one.** X-42A was allocated in the same months the
contract began, which makes the pairing better founded than the X-41 case examined in the preceding
article, and it was then never used officially again, which makes it worse founded than any confirmed
designation. Four years later the same number was applied informally to a winged reusable booster that
had little but its contractor in common with the stage, and the authoritative survey now declines to tie
the number to either\[[USFE X-42][ref_x42_parsch]\]. **Three of the four articles from the X-39 onward have found a doubtful pairing of
designation and vehicle**, which makes the pattern a matter of how the number space was
administered in the late 1990s.

**What survives is the data.** The stage is gone, the designation is unattached, and the two things the
programme was built to demonstrate, being a peroxide and hydrocarbon engine at useful thrust and a
composite common-bulkhead tank compatible with concentrated peroxide, both reached ground test before
the programme ended. **That is a reasonable return for a vehicle that never left the ground.**
